study.title: Matthew 26 The betrayal, the supper, the agony, and the denial of Jesus
study.overview: Matthew 26 presents the approach of Jesus" passion with strong contrast between human wickedness and the fulfillment of God's plan. The religious leaders plot their death; a woman honors him with an expensive perfume; Judas negotiates his surrender; Jesus prepares the Passover and institutes the supper as a sign of the new covenant; then, in Gethsemane, submits to the will of the Father in deep distress; finally, he is imprisoned, falsely judged and Peter repeatedly denies him. The chapter shows that the cross is not an accident, but the way in which Jesus performs redemption, while the disciples reveal their fragility.

outline.title: The conspiracy against Jesus and the anointing in Bethany
outline.explanation: Jesus announces that his surrender is near. As the religious leaders plan to arrest and kill him, a woman unfrorns him with valuable perfume. The indignation of the disciples is corrected by Jesus, who interprets the gesture as preparation for burial and as an act worthy of memory throughout the world. Then Judas proceeds to negotiate the treason for silver.

outline.title: Easter, the betrayal announced and the supper of the new covenant
outline.explanation: Jesus directs the disciples to prepare the Passover and meets with the twelve. During the meal, he announces that he will be betrayed and reveals the gravity of the betrayer's guilt, even though his way is written in the Scriptures. Then Jesus takes bread and cup and associates them with his body and blood, speaking of the new covenant and forgiveness of sins.

outline.title: Gethsemane, the submission to the Father and the prison
outline.explanation: Jesus predicts the dispersion of the disciples and the denial of Peter, but also proclaims his resurrection. In Gethsemane, he prays in intense sorrow, asking that the cup pass, but submitting to the will of the Father. The disciples sleep instead of watching. Judas arrives with the armed crowd, identifies Jesus with a kiss and he is imprisoned; when a disciple reacts with the sword, Jesus corrects him, stating that his prison fulfills the Scriptures.

outline.title: Religious Judgment and Denial of Peter
outline.explanation: Jesus is taken to the house of the high priest, where authorities seek false testimony to condemn him. Two accusations are highlighted, and the high priest questions him about his messianic and divine identity. Jesus responds solemnly, alluding to the enthronement and glorious coming of the Son of man. Condemned, he suffers insults. Meanwhile, Peter follows him from afar, but before three successive accusations denies him with oaths; then the cock sings, he remembers the word of Jesus and weeps bitterly.

study.context: The chapter occurs in the environment of Easter and the unleavened loaves, feasts linked to the memory of Israel's liberation. The notes provided highlight that the Passover remembered the deliverance in Egypt and that the supper of Jesus points to a new covenant. It is also mentioned that the meeting of the leaders in the house of Caiaphas was urgent and probably reserved, and that Peter's reaction, upon hearing the singing of the rooster, brought him back to the word of Jesus.
study.theology: Matthew 26 emphasizes that the death of Jesus is both unjust and necessary in God's plan. He is the Son of man who will be judged by evil people, but his surrender fulfills the Scriptures. His blood inaugurates the new covenant and is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, showing that salvation does not come by human merit, but by the substitutional offering of Christ. The anointing in Bethany points to his imminent death; Gethsemane reveals his true humanity, with deep sorrow, and his perfect obedience to the Father. The chapter also denounces the weakness of the disciples: Peter's self-confidence, sleep at the moment of vigilance and general abandonment show that discipleship depends on the grace of God, not of natural courage. At the same time, Jesus' response to suffering and betrayal manifests his authority: he is not a passive victim, but the Lord who surrenders voluntarily and moves to fulfill the Father's will.

scholarViews.insight: The death of Jesus is presented with irony: the Son of man, who judges the nations, is first judged unjustly; his death is understood as the definitive paschal sacrifice.
The paschal supper is followed by the establishment of the memorial of Christ's sacrificial death, which the church must remember through this gesture.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the difference between the human way of evaluating people and the way Jesus evaluate the surrender to him?
How does the Lord's supper in this text correct superficial ideas about Christ's forgiveness, covenant, and memory?
In which areas my self-confidence resembles that of Peter, and how can I learn to watch and pray more seriously?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to humility and vigilance. Apply it like this: 1) love Jesus for having willingly surrendered to the forgiveness of sins; 2) examine whether his devotion is sincere like that of Bethany's wife or just criticism like that of the disciples; 3) practice prayer before the pressures and temptations, remembering that the spirit may be willing, but the flesh is weak; 4) when it fails, as Peter, does not remain in the fall, but let the word of Christ lead it to true repentance.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided offer some historical data on Caiaphas, the Passover and the interpretation of the supper; outside of this, this study avoids adding information not backed by them. The text also allusions to parallel passages in the other gospels, but here were used only as interpretive support indicated in the notes, without trying to harmonize all the details. Some expressions of the biblical text may reflect the writing of the Free Bible, and the explanation was maintained at the level of the general sense of the chapter.
